1:
They arrive at Iconium out of a defeat, and two of them say so. Calvin admits the beginning might seem unprosperous, since they were expelled from Antioch and forced to shake the dust from their feet; yet they do not yield, because the Lord called them upon that condition, that they should do their duty though the whole world and Satan said nay. They came not only ready to teach, he says, but armed to enter conflicts, and what was spoken to Jeremiah is common to all the ministers of God, that they shall fight against thee but shall not prevail: they were furnished for continual warfare, not one combat. Henry says it in his own idiom: as the blood of the martyrs has been the seed of the church, so the banishment of the confessors has scattered that seed. Though the Jews at Antioch had used them barbarously they did not decline preaching to the Jews at Iconium, and Henry draws the rule: let none of any denomination be condemned in the gross, but let us do good to those who have done evil to us. Wesley compresses it into six words: persecution having increased their strength. Gill notes only the speed, that it was at the first opportunity.

That they went in both together carries much weight for Henry and none for Calvin. Henry makes it deliberate: they went together to testify their unanimity and mutual affection, that people might say, see how they love one another; that they might strengthen one another’s hands, and that out of the mouth of two witnesses every word might be established. Calvin refers the Greek phrase to the Jews instead, and so removes the foundation Henry built on: not that Paul and Barnabas went in together, but that they followed the multitude at the appointed time of meeting, so that they spoke not secretly with a few but in a great assembly. Robertson stands between them, noting the phrase and its parallel elsewhere, and adds that it was a tremendous first meeting.

On the manner of the speaking they agree, then divide over what to credit. Barnes says they spake with such power that their preaching was attended by the influence of the Spirit, and Clarke says the same. Henry lingers: they so spoke, so plainly, so warmly, with such manifest concern for the souls of men, that one might perceive they were not only convinced but filled with the things they spoke of, and what came from the heart was likely to reach the heart. Then he takes the credit back: the success was not to be attributed to the manner but to the Spirit of God, who made use of that means. Calvin arrives there by arithmetic. One only sermon was not without fruit, and if one or two had believed they might have thought they sped well, but the Lord confirmeth them far better when they gather such plentiful fruit in a short time: they knew that so many hearts were converted not so much by their voice as by the power of the Spirit. Robertson reads the result clause as stating an actual result, not a possible one.

Who the Greeks were, three settle the same way. Ellicott says the term is used in its wider sense, equivalent to Gentile, though it implies that those so described spoke and understood Greek, and that here they would be the proselytes of the gate who heard the Apostles in the synagogue. Barnes and Clarke agree, Clarke setting genuine descendants of the twelve tribes against proselytes of the gate. Henry sees the two put together for the first time: in the previous chapter the gospel went first to the Jews and then to the Gentiles, but here they stand on the same level, the Jews not so losing their preference as to be thrown behind.
2:
The trouble starts where Ellicott says it nearly always starts: it is the distinguishing feature of almost all the persecutions in Acts, he says, that they originated in the hostility of the Jews; the case of Demetrius is almost the only exception, and even there they fomented the enmity of the Greek craftsmen, and a century later they are still prominent in the persecution that killed Polycarp at Smyrna. Calvin gives the same reading a figure: they were firebrands to inflame the minds of the Gentiles, who could have borne the gospel had these fans not kindled their resistance. Gill fixes which Jews are meant, that part continuing in unbelief; Clarke which Gentiles, mere heathens as against the proselytes.

Two words are weighed. Robertson corrects the text first, the participle being aorist, not the present the Received Text prints, then declines to press the sense: strictly one Greek verb means to disobey and another to disbelieve, but the distinction is not observed elsewhere, the word meaning to be unwilling to be persuaded, and so to withhold belief and then obedience: the two run into one another, for to disbelieve the word of God is to disobey God. On made their minds evil affected he finds an old verb meaning to ill-treat, used in later Greek for to embitter, in that sense only here in the New Testament; Barnes and Clarke render it irritated or exasperated, Calvin as to infect with malicious affection or to enforce to do hurt. On the brethren, Barnes and Clarke agree it was a common name for the disciples before they were called Christians at Antioch. Calvin takes it wider, that Luke comprehends all the godly, so that every convert was vexed as if a pernicious sect had risen to shake the public state — then concedes: if any had rather restrain it unto Paul and Barnabas, I am not greatly against him.

Robertson alone leaves the text for the legend. Codex Bezae adds that the synagogue chiefs and the rulers brought the persecution on; and the story of Thecla, located at Iconium, may hint at the means, the apostles perhaps charged with interference with family life and acquitted. The story has apocryphal features, he grants, though Thecla may be historical, and its portrait of Paul cannot be authentic though a true tradition may underlie it: bald, bowlegged, small in stature, with meeting eyebrows, sometimes looking like a man and sometimes having the face of an angel.

The long stay and the miracles go together. Barnes notices no forcible measures to expel them as at Antioch, so they regarded it their duty to remain, and that persecution is often attended with signal success. Ellicott will not have less than several months, in which the two worked for their livelihood, and locates the boldness in a full declaration of the gospel of grace against the narrowing Judaism the proselytes had known; Robertson guesses six months and warns that such a season could not last, some manuscripts adding that the next outbreak came a second time. On what the signs were for, three converge. Ellicott says the miracles came as the confirmation of faith, not its foundation. Clarke says no apostle could work one by himself, the power not resident in them but granted when a miracle was needed. Calvin says the same of the agency, that they are not properly Paul and Barnabas’s miracles but God’s alone, who so works by men that he will not have his glory darkened; and he makes the clause a rule, that God never suffers miracles to be separated from his word. On that rule he attacks those who lead the world from the gospel by bare miracles, to call upon the dead, burn incense to idols, undertake vowed pilgrimages. Barnes keeps to the giver: the testimony was borne by the Lord Jesus, bodily absent yet clothed with power.
4:
The city splits, and the question is whose fault that is. Robertson takes the Greek for a schism of the kind made by Sadducees and Pharisees, and puts the division within the Gentile populace, the Jewish leaders having made some impression as at Pisidian Antioch. Ellicott reads it of the heathen population, and assumes the converts were a minority from the lower classes, the chief men and women of the city against them. Gill has them divided in their sentiments, some approving the doctrines and miracles, others condemning them as false delusions; Clarke sorts them by disposition, those who had not hardened their hearts feeling the force of the truth and, without prejudice, discerning the miracles to be God’s. Barnes and Calvin both refuse to charge the gospel with the split. A revival of religion may produce excitement by the bad passions of opposers, Barnes says, but the fault is not in Christianity; it lies with those who confederate against it. Calvin puts it as a rule: the discord flowed from the gospel, than which nothing is more contrary to discord, but the forwardness of men makes the bond of unity an occasion of tumults, so soon as any schism ariseth, before we condemn those who seem to be its authors, it behoveth us to consider who ought to bear the blame. He goes further: as that unity is accursed which separates us from God, better that a few depart an hundred times from the world and come into favour with God than keep peace with it while disagreeing with him. Robertson pauses instead on the title, this being the first place in Acts where Paul and Barnabas are called apostles; since the book elsewhere keeps the word for the twelve, Luke cannot mean it in the technical sense that required sight of the Risen Christ.

Who the rulers were is the one open dispute. Robertson keeps them to the synagogue, since the city officials would hardly join such a mob, though he reports two scholars who think the magistrates were involved, as at Pisidian Antioch. Ellicott reaches the same rulers by the form of punishment, which makes them synagogue rulers and the charge, as with Stephen, blasphemy. Clarke will not choose, and has both the heathen rulers and the synagogue rulers in it. On the assault Barnes and Robertson divide by a shade: Barnes reads a rush denoting impetuous aggression, a popular tumult rather than a deliberate purpose, while Robertson thinks it denotes not the attack so much as its open start, adding that the plan to stone shows the Jews in the lead and the rabble following: legal proceedings having failed, the only resource left was illegal violence. Gill reduces it to a strong bias and inclination in the minds.

On the word for despiteful usage the lexical voices agree, and one turns it back on Paul. It expresses wanton insult and outrage, Ellicott says, and Paul uses the noun formed from it of his own conduct as persecutor, so that in the stoning a few verses later he must have felt he was receiving the just reward of his deeds. Barnes glosses it as to reproach, to bring contempt upon, to injure; Clarke expands it into a programme, to make them appear monsters or movers of sedition, then stone them for the alleged crime. Calvin uses the flight to define courage. They give not back when their enemies merely set themselves against them, he says, but when the sedition waxes hot and they are in danger of stoning they go no further, remembering that in patience the faithful possess their souls; and though they fly, their preaching elsewhere declares that they feared not danger. This is the right kind of fear, he concludes, when the servants of Christ do not run wilfully into their enemies’ hands, and yet do not abandon their duty.
6:
The flight is read by four of them as obedience rather than retreat. Barnes says that though persecuted they still preached, and though driven from one city fled into another, which was the direction of the Saviour; Ellicott says we can scarcely fail to trace a literal obedience to our Lord’s commands. Robertson agrees and puts it bluntly: they had no idea of remaining to be lynched by this mob, and it is a wise preacher who always knows when to stand his ground and when to leave for the glory of God. Gill has them weighing it, apprised of the plot and considering what was best at this juncture; Clarke notes that they did not leave the province but went to other towns in it.

Where those towns lie no two of them agree. Clarke puts Lystra to the south and Derbe to the north of Iconium, according to the general opinion. Barnes puts Lystra a few miles south of Iconium and Derbe a short distance east of Lystra. Ellicott stretches the distances, Lystra about forty miles to the south-east and Derbe twenty miles further east, and identifies Lystra with a ruin-field called the thousand and one churches, under a conical black mountain. Robertson has an inscription, which puts Lystra some eighteen miles south-southwest of Iconium, and concedes that the site of Derbe is really not known. Clarke alone raises a second puzzle: how comes it that Luke does not call Iconium a city of Lycaonia as well as Derbe and Lystra, when the ancient geographers place it there, one describing the Lycaonian hills as plain, cold and naked, pastures for wild asses, with Iconium on a better soil? He answers from another ancient author, that a tetrarchy of fourteen cities was granted out of Lycaonia on the side bordering Galatia, Iconium the most famous of them.

The country itself gets one long description and one short one. Ellicott calls it wilder and less civilised, cut off by the Taurus from the cultivated country, a dreary plain bare of trees, destitute of fresh water and dotted with salt lakes, and quotes a Roman poet who had seen it: where men once dwelt a marshy lake is seen, and coots and bitterns haunt the waters green. Then he presses the name: Lycaonia was traditionally interpreted as Wolf-land, from the legend of a man transformed into a wolf, and represented but too faithfully, he says, the character of the inhabitants. Robertson quotes a flatter verdict, a high table land, ill-watered, bleak, but suited for sheep pasture.

On what kind of ground they had come to, Ellicott and Robertson pull apart. Ellicott has them losing the protection a Roman citizen might claim, Lycaonia having been annexed to Galatia and then assigned away to a client king; so wild a country was hardly likely to attract Jewish settlers, and since the narrative shows no synagogue in either city, here for the first time, so far as we know, Paul had to begin by preaching to the heathen. Robertson keeps them inside the empire: the cities were still part of the province of Galatia, Lystra had been made a colony, Derbe was the frontier city in the south-east, and the new imperial road from Antioch and Iconium reached them both — evidence, he says, that Paul kept to his plan of going to centres of influence. He adds a difficulty nobody else raises, that the work must have been done with help from disciples of Antioch and Iconium, since neither man could speak Lycaonian. Gill and Clarke both report the same addition at the end of the verse, that the whole multitude were moved at their preaching and Paul and Barnabas tarried at Lystra; Gill adds that no church in either place is heard of until the sixth century, when the bishops of Lystra and Derbe attended a Roman synod.
8:
The sign is placed deliberately, and they say why. Henry sets it beside the cure wrought by Peter and John: that one introduced the gospel among the Jews, this among the Gentiles, and both were designed to represent the impotency of all men in spiritual things, who are lame from their birth till the grace of God puts strength into them, since it was while we were yet without strength that Christ died for the ungodly. Barnes gives a reason of policy: persecuted from place to place and opposed in every manner, they wanted a signal miracle to carry forward and establish the work. Calvin assumes this was one of many, reported alone because of what followed, and counts the circumstances that set forth the power of God: the man never walked, he was suddenly healed by the voice of Paul alone before the eyes of all, and legs which were dead were made nimble, so that he leapt up without any stop.

Whether he was begging is disputed on one word. Gill supposes he sat there to beg, where there was a great concourse; Barnes says the word sat indicates his usual posture and helpless condition, such persons commonly sitting by the wayside to ask alms. Henry refuses the inference: it does not appear he was a beggar, since it is said that he sat, not that he sat begging. Robertson lands with Henry: he was no mendicant pretender, his history being known from his birth. Ellicott notes the writer’s care to record how long the infirmity had lasted. Clarke alone tries a diagnosis: the man had no muscular power, and probably his ankle bones were dislocated, or he had what is commonly termed club feet, the likelier since he never walked.

Where the faith came from they answer alike. Clarke asks how faith came to this poor heathen and replies, by hearing the word preached, for it is said the same heard Paul speak; and he must besides have heard of the miracles already wrought. Gill notes that one version adds that he cried out to Paul. Calvin observes that hearing is set down first, so that we may know the faith was conceived of Paul’s doctrine. Ellicott presses the tense: he used to listen to Paul as he spoke, and so had been among his hearers some days, had heard the gospel of the death and resurrection, and had found such a Saviour met his every need. Robertson reads the same imperfect and reports the guess that he was a proselyte. Wesley makes shortest work of it: he felt the power of God in his soul, and thence knew it sufficient to heal his body also.

How Paul knew is where they part. Barnes says it is not stated, and guesses the ardour and desire in the man’s countenance; Ellicott has the Apostle read it in the upward look with that earnest gaze of his; Robertson says Paul saw a new hope in his eyes and face. Calvin rejects the method. We know how deceitful a thing the countenance of man is, he says, and no sure judgment of faith could be given by it, faith having God alone to be witness; the cripple’s faith was revealed to Paul by the secret inspiration of the Spirit. He then guards the case from becoming a rule: this was a singular motion of the Spirit, many may receive the gospel and yet not be cured of the diseases that vex them, and this faith, which gives room for miracles, is a particular one that many of God’s children want who are yet endued with the Spirit of adoption. Ellicott concedes as much, calling faith the general though not universal law of miraculous working. Henry, who has no such reservation, says only that God will not disappoint the desires of his own kindling, nor the hopes of his own raising.
10:
The command and the leap are read for their speed. Robertson says the usual English conceals the picture: he leaped up with a single bound and began to walk, upright being the physicians’ word for erect. Gill and Robertson explain the loud voice by the audience, that all might hear; Calvin adds that Paul raised it so the sudden change might the more move the multitude, and reads the leap as a prepared mind, the man walking already in mind while his feet were yet dead. On the clause some copies add, in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, the two differ only about the text: Clarke thinks the evidence too weak, though Paul surely used the name; Calvin thinks Luke wrote it.

The speech of Lycaonia divides them. Barnes takes it for a mixture of Greek and Syriac, the Greek of the region corrupted by the nearness of Syria. Clarke rules that out on the face of the verse, since Luke distinguishes it from Greek, reports two scholarly guesses, and gives up: every search after the language of Lycaonia must at this distance of time be fruitless. Ellicott says only that it is held to have affinities with Assyrian, and that a people of two tongues would use their own to each other and Greek to strangers. Then Ellicott turns the detail into an argument: Luke records it to account for the passivity of the Apostles until the words bore fruit in acts, and it is almost a crucial instance that the gift of tongues, which Paul possessed so largely, did not include every provincial dialect he met; to suppose instead that they understood and let the preparations proceed for a more dramatic protest is at variance with the narrative and with any worthy view of Paul’s character. Robertson agrees from the story: Paul understood the part assigned him only when the sacrifice was being got ready.

On why the cry took that form, two reach for the same page of Homer. Barnes says it was common to suppose the gods appeared in human shape, that being the only way they were thought to take knowledge of human affairs, and quotes the lines about gods who can with ease all shapes assume, repairing to populous cities to mark the deeds of men; Clarke quotes the identical lines in the identical English, adds Ovid on Jupiter coming down disguised to test the report of the age, and observes that it seems copied from the Lord going down to see Sodom. Clarke traces the whole family of fictions to the angels who visited Abraham, Jacob and Lot; Calvin had said the same two centuries earlier, the poets turning into fables what the fathers taught of angels. Ellicott and Robertson supply the local legend: Zeus and Hermes had come in human guise into this region and been entertained by Baucis and Philemon, the place kept afterwards as a shrine; and Zeus had a temple at Lystra.

What the mistake shows is answered twice. Calvin makes it a lesson about miracles: Paul had spoken not abruptly but as the conclusion of a sermon concerning Christ, and the people ascribed the praise to their idols as if they had heard no word of it, which is why the Lord would have few miracles wrought and those for a short time, lest men’s lust drag them to a contrary end. He adds a lesson about upbringing: they prefer Barnabas to Paul only from the childish surmise about Mercury the interpreter of the gods in which they were bred, and errors learned in youth are so hard to root out that the works of God only harden them. Wesley sets the two halves of the world against each other: the Jews would not own Christ’s Godhead though they saw him work numberless miracles, while the heathen, seeing mere men work one, deified them at once.
12:
Which apostle got which god is settled by their bodies. Gill has Barnabas oldest, tallest and bulkiest, the best figure, while Paul was younger, of low stature and mean appearance; Robertson says Barnabas was older and more imposing, and that Paul admits he was not impressive in looks. Barnes and Clarke both credit an early Greek father with the same conjecture, Barnabas a large athletic man and Paul small in person. Ellicott makes the contrast a matter of art: unlike as the Apostle’s weak bodily presence was to the sandalled messenger’s sculptured grace, something in the taller and more stately Barnabas may have suggested Jupiter. But he cautions that the masterpieces of Greek art were unlikely to reach a Lycaonian village, so the Hermes of Lystra may have stood to that of Athens as the grotesque Madonna of a wayside shrine does to a master’s. Real idolatry cares little for the beauty of what it worships, he says, and these were genuine idolaters.

The other half is eloquence, and here Clarke finds what the rest do not. Mercury was the god of speech, and the very phrase used of Paul, the leader of the discourse, was a standing title of Hermes: Clarke produces two ancient authors, one calling Hermes the god who is leader of words, the other that Mercury is powerful in voice and eloquence. Robertson says Paul was clearly the leader of the talk, so it seemed a clear case to the natives, and adds that it would be something if preachers always knew what people really think of them. Barnes puts the office plainly, Mercury delivering the messages of the gods while Paul only had been discoursing, then catalogues the rest: patron of travellers and shepherds, conductor of the dead, president over orators and merchants, and god of thieves and all dishonest persons.

On the phrase which was before their city, two converge from opposite directions. Clarke argues it is a technical title. Cities were put under a deity whose image stood at the entrance, and each attribute of a god had its own priests and rites, Jupiter the thunderer having a different service from Jove the guardian; Luke’s phrase renders the guardian’s title exactly, which Clarke takes for evidence of his accuracy. Ellicott confirms it from the stones: the identical phrase is found in Greek inscriptions at Ephesus. Barnes and Gill settle only the grammar, that the words describe Jupiter and not the priest, Gill noting that one version makes him the chief god of their city and another places him outside it; Wesley has temple and image just without the gate.

What was brought, and why, is disputed at both ends. Barnes supposes two oxen, one for each, and takes the gates for the city gates where the images stood; Ellicott takes them for the folding-doors of the courtyard where the Apostles lodged, and calls the garlands the white woollen fillets of sculpture. Robertson and Wesley put the garlands on the oxen; Clarke, after quoting Ovid and Virgil on gilded horns and fillets, will not decide whether they were meant for the oxen or the apostles, and says the Lycaonians behaved as Hindoo priests still do. Calvin alone asks after the priest’s motive. Luke does not say what moved him, but there was hope of plentiful gain: if it were noised abroad that Jupiter had appeared there, the opinion would follow that he was more delighted in the temple of Lystra than any other, and men spare no cost once such superstition fills their minds. The world is inclined to it of itself, he says, but then come the sacrificing priests, who are like fans and bellows; and the multitude was moved by ambition too, that their city might be more famous. Hence Satan has such liberty to deceive, while the priests set nets for gain and the people are delighted to have errors confirmed.
14:
The torn clothes are treated as evidence. Chrysostom marks the vehemence — they rent their clothes, ran in, cried out, all from strong affection of the soul, since it was a grief inconsolable that they should be thought gods and introduce the very idolatry they came to destroy. Ellicott turns the act into an argument: it is recorded as the act of men startled and surprised, altogether incompatible with the theory that they knew they had been taken for deities and were expecting such honours; it was the extremest expression of horror, hardly ever used except against blasphemy, and though the heathen may not have understood it, its strangeness would arrest them. Robertson agrees drily that it was strange conduct for the supposed gods. Calvin will not let them off with words: they troubled the sacrifice as much as they were able, whereas hypocrites who refuse honour only provoke the simple to press it harder by their feigned modesty. This is holy anger, he says: a pastor must be as vigilant for his Lord’s glory as a husband for his wife’s chastity; and when the world abuses the names of holy men unto superstition it thinks to please them, but they will stand up first against their own worshippers.

The verse also calls Barnabas an apostle, and three of them explain it away. Gill says he is even placed before Paul, not as greater, but from the opinion these heathens had of him. Barnes says he is called one because sent forth by the church on a particular errand, not as a witness to the resurrection. Calvin says the word is stretched beyond the order Christ appointed, the two being properly evangelists.

On men of like passions Clarke loses his temper with an earlier commentator. The saying has been most strangely perverted, he says, by taking passion in its vulgar sense of bad temper or evil propensity, as though these holy men were confessing sinful infirmities; the words mean no more than that they are truly human beings with the same powers and appetites, needing food and raiment and mortal like the rest. Barnes says the same without the heat, the Latin rendering it simply, we are mortal like yourselves; Robertson makes it of like nature, affected by like sensations, not gods at all; Ellicott notes the parallel with Peter’s words to Cornelius. Barnes then does what none of the others do. The abhorrence shown here throws light on the rank of Christ: worship offered to Paul and Barnabas was refused with indignation, yet when Thomas said My Lord and my God there was commendation and not the slightest reproof; how is the difference to be accounted for except that the Lord Jesus was divine?

The word vanities is pressed by all. Ellicott hears a gesture in the demonstrative, the Apostle pointing at the pomp of the sacrifice, and sets the one God against the polytheism that parcelled out heaven and earth and sea and the pantheism that excluded will and purpose from the Godhead. Robertson says the same of the pointing, and that they must go the whole way, our God being live and not a dead statue. Wesley notes that Paul does not deign to call them gods, and that each region named had its own. Barnes observes how new the doctrine was: they worshipped multitudes of divinities and never conceived all things formed from nothing by one Infinite Being. Clarke marvels at the boldness of saying it before a mob engaged in a rite they thought the state’s safety hung on. Chrysostom notices what is left out, nothing of things invisible and nowhere the name of Christ, because they had learnt to study not what is worthy of God but what is profitable for the hearers. Calvin takes the word as a definition: all religion is vain which departs from the pure and simple Word of God.
16:
The clause about past ages is where two of them find a philosophy of history, using the phrase independently. Ellicott calls it the first germ of Paul’s: the times of ignorance were permitted, those who lived in them to be judged by their knowledge, the sins of the Gentile world running their course as the Law did its partial work among the Jews, both brought to feel the need of redemption. Robertson says Paul touches God in history as he had just touched him in creation, and that this does not mean God was ignorant or unconcerned: he was biding his time in patience. Clarke and Ellicott both correct the rendering to all the Gentiles, Clarke adding that the Jews, having a revelation, were not left to walk in their own ways. Then Barnes and Calvin part over whether the reason may be asked. Barnes says we cannot determine it and at once offers three: to show the insufficiency of reason in religion, the experiment having run four thousand years with the most enlightened nations failing no less than the most degraded; to show the need of revelation; and to evince man’s depravity. Calvin refuses the question: they show no cause why the Lord suffered the world to err so long, and we must count his will alone the chiefest law of equity, wondering reverently at a counsel oftentimes hid from us.

On the witness God left, Ellicott notices the audience: to peasants Paul dwells on the goodness manifested in nature, while at Athens and Rome he points philosophers to the fuller witness of consciousness and conscience. He then makes a conjecture out of the rhythm: the words from giving us rain from heaven are so rhythmical that Paul may be quoting a hymn heard at a harvest or vintage festival, claiming it, as he claimed the altar to the Unknown God, for the God men ignorantly worshipped. Robertson adds that Zeus was the rain-god and Lycaonia often dry, so the item was well chosen.

The rain draws the best writing out of three. Barnes says man could not cause it and without it the earth would be one wide desolation, then turns the argument on ignorance: the sun and stars move by fixed laws whose operation we can see and anticipate, but the falling of rain and dew is regulated by laws we cannot trace, and seems poured directly from God’s hollow hand. Calvin argues from the same order the other way, that heaven and earth are not moved by their own motion, much less by fortune, and that God has not set man on earth as an idle beholder seated in a theatre, but to exercise himself in praising the liberality of God. Clarke finds the proof in the measure: God gives never less than is necessary nor more than is sufficient, preventing luxury by one limit and discontent by the other. Wesley has Paul pointing upward as he says from heaven, and adds that God testifies of himself by punishments too, but more peculiarly by benefits.

How far the witness reaches is the last question. Calvin draws the line: such testimony made men without excuse yet was not sufficient to salvation, faith being conceived not by the bare beholding of heaven and earth but by the hearing of the word. Clarke agrees on the first half, those who went on worshipping stocks and stones being without excuse; Ellicott leans the other way, that those in the times of ignorance would be equitably dealt with. On the filling of hearts Barnes notes the Hebraism, hearts for persons, and Calvin that God gives more than necessity requires, food not only to refresh strength but to make the heart merry; Gill observes that they had not the written law but were not destitute of the law of nature, the goodness that should have led them to repentance being abused instead.
18:
That the crowd was only just held off is read two ways. Calvin takes it for a measure of how untamed the heat of the world is toward idolatry: if they believed these men gods, why not believe their word when it put false honour from them? All idolaters are sick of this disease, ready to shake off the yoke unless religion be subject to their own will. Robertson calls it a harrowing ordeal in which Paul had at last won, if only nobody else had interposed. Ellicott looks at the same crowd and sees converts: on some the effect may have been that they turned from vanities to the living God, and the work at Lystra must have lasted long enough to found a church, among its converts Lois, Eunice and the young Timothy. Gill glosses these sayings as the words about themselves and about the living God.

Then the wind turns, and six reach for the same antithesis. Henry puts it shortest: today Hosanna, tomorrow Crucify; today sacrificed to, tomorrow sacrificed. Had Paul consented to be Mercury he might have been enthroned, nay enshrined; because he will be a faithful minister of Christ he is stoned and cast out. Popular breath, Henry says, turns like the wind. Calvin says almost the same, that Paul might have reigned under the title of Mercury with the commendation of all men, and is stoned because he serves Christ faithfully. Barnes calls it a striking instance of the uselessness of mere popularity, and adds that it was well for Paul that he was not seeking it. Robertson says the pendulum swings easily from one extreme to the other; Wesley needs nine words, moved with equal ease either to adore or murder him. And Henry, Clarke and Ellicott all reach independently for the same later scene, the islanders who took Paul first for a murderer and then for a god, the reversal run backwards.

Who did it, and how far they came, is set out by two. Ellicott identifies the Pisidian Antioch and measures the distance: the Jews of the two cities acted in concert, those of the further having travelled not less than a hundred and thirty miles to hinder the work. Robertson guesses they were travelling grain merchants, or followed the fine Roman road on purpose to keep the two on the run, striking at the psychological moment. Barnes draws the reproach: persecutors show a zeal in a bad cause which it were well if Christians showed in a good one, and men will travel farther to do evil than good. Clarke says what they could not do themselves they got others to do. Henry explains why Paul and not Barnabas, the chief speaker having galled them more; Robertson puts it in the language of the scene: they stoned Mercury and passed over Jupiter. Ellicott presses the manner: stoning shows the thing planned by Jews satisfying themselves that they punished a blasphemer, casting him out to be buried with the burial of an ass; the blinding blows fell on him as on Stephen, so that in one sense the martyr expiated the guilt of the persecutor.

Whether he died they cannot agree. Clarke says they did not leave off stoning until they had fullest evidence of death, and so most probably he was dead. Barnes says the next verse shows he was not, though many commentators and the Jews supposed he was and was miraculously restored. Robertson observes only that Luke does not say he was dead. Henry takes the middle: not dead, but ill crushed and bruised and fallen into a swoon, so that it was not without a miracle that he came so soon to himself and could walk back into the city. Calvin will have the account kept as a death, since as touching himself he suffered a most cruel death and was wonderfully delivered by the Lord.
20:
Who was standing round him, and why, is filled in four ways. Gill takes them for the young converts of Lystra, weeping and lamenting and, it may be, praying that God would restore him to life, their presence showing affection to their spiritual father. Clarke has them in earnest prayer, entreating the Author of life that his soul might return to its battered tenement. Ellicott says they had been powerless to stop the attack but stole out when it was over, perhaps to give him a decent interment, and thinks Lois, Eunice and Timothy were in that crowd, weeping first for sorrow and then for joy. Robertson adds that Timothy, a lad of about fifteen, would not soon forget the scene. Barnes reads the circle differently: they do not seem to have supposed him dead, but may have expected him to revive.

Whether the recovery was a miracle is the sharpest quarrel in the chapter, and Barnes conducts it by name. Most commentators have supposed a miracle, he says, holding that Paul could not have risen so soon and walked into the city without one, and he names Calvin and Clarke among them, both here. But they assert what the sacred penman does not intimate, he replies, and there is no propriety in supposing miraculous agency where it is not necessary: the probability is that he was stunned by a single blow and recovered after a short time, nothing being more common than to be rendered apparently lifeless by a blow on the head. His two named opponents hold their ground. Calvin says it appeareth plainly that Paul was miraculously saved, since next morning, cast out for dead, he takes his journey fresh and sound; Clarke says he was restored not only to life but to perfect soundness. Wesley presses hardest, calling it a miracle little less than a resurrection, and gives the reason from procedure: the witnesses threw the first and largest stone they could lift, with all possible violence, upon the head, enough of itself to dash the skull in pieces, and the people then joined as long as any token of life remained. Robertson slips the word in parenthetically, apparently a miraculous recovery; Ellicott stands with Barnes, that the teacher was stunned only, and not dead.

The journey next day is measured twice, and the two disagree. Ellicott puts Derbe twenty miles east of Lystra, its exact site unidentified, and notes the region infamous for brigandage, so the perils of robbers Paul afterwards lists may refer to it; he insists too on the cost of the walk, several hours of hardship after the suffering of the day before. Robertson makes it some forty miles, near the pass to the Cilician Gates. Calvin uses the journey as proof of temper: Paul creeps not into a corner where, like an overworn soldier, he may live idly, but goes back to the places where he was cruelly handled a little before.

On the return the readings divide between courage and calculation. Barnes calls it a remarkable instance of courage, the welfare of the infant churches weighing more than their own safety. Clarke says behold the courage of these Christian men: one who knows he is God’s ambassador has nothing but his God to fear. Robertson agrees it was necessary work, to see the churches could withstand persecution, and notes that Paul was a Roman citizen who had not yet used the privilege, which would count for little against a mob. Ellicott lowers the temperature: the work at Derbe implies a stay of some months, in which the hostility at Antioch and Iconium had probably subsided, so the two could retrace their steps without great danger. Calvin draws a lesson from the confirming: the use of the Word is not instruction alone, and pastors have not done their duty in training their people in knowledge unless they also admonish and exhort.
22:
Confirming is a word three of them are careful to disarm. Barnes says it has in some churches a technical sense, admission to full privileges by imposition of hands, and that the word here refers to no such rite: whether that rite has New Testament authority or not, it gets no support from this passage. Ellicott says the same more mildly, preferring strengthening so as to avoid the associations of the other term, the Greek not being the word later writers use of the rite. Robertson glosses it as making more firm, and notes that in Acts the word is used of these churches every time. Clarke turns the noun into a picture: disciple means a scholar, and the Church was a school with Christ for chief Master and the apostles for subordinate teachers; but information is of little avail if the heart is not disciplined, and so it was the souls that were confirmed. Gill fences the word from the other side: not their bodies, the physician’s business, nor their estates, the magistrate’s, but their souls.

What the faith means two settle the same way. Ellicott asks whether it is used subjectively, of the feeling of trust, or objectively, of the substance of what was believed, and judges the latter probable, that sense being established a few years after Luke wrote. Clarke had assumed it, arguing that since there must be a standard of truth to resort to, they needed a system of doctrine known to come from God, called The Faith. On must Barnes enters a caution: not that it is fixed by any fatal necessity, but that such is the nature of religion and the wickedness of the world that it will happen, and we are to calculate on it. Calvin widens the word past persecution to all the sorrows the life of the godly is subject to, and notes that while God oftentimes spares the wicked and fats them with prosperity he is sharper toward his own.

The pronoun in we must is where Ellicott and Robertson part. Ellicott finds it suggestive and asks whether Luke is generalising what he heard from Paul’s hearers and giving it in their words, or was himself one of them, the two having clearly met before we find them together at Troas. Robertson denies that anything follows, the sentence being a general proposition applying to all Christians at all times, and adds that Timothy might as easily have told Luke about the work; it all sounds, he says, like a quotation of Paul’s very language.

Then the word rendered ordained, where three stand on one side and Ellicott on the other. Barnes says the verb properly means to stretch out the hand, and since it was customary to elect that way it means simply to elect; that Paul and Barnabas did it means probably that they presided while the church chose by suffrage. Clarke distinguishes two Greek words, one the stretching out of hands in approval, the other the laying on of hands, quotes an old canonist on how the first came to mean the second, and concludes that anciently the people chose the pastor and the rulers appointed him, both being thought necessary. Calvin asks whether the two do this alone by their private office, and answers that they suffer the matter to be decided by the consent of all, the people having free election while the apostles sit as chief moderators lest a tumult arise. Ellicott grants that popular election is the natural meaning and sets it aside: the word is used here of the two Apostles, not of the Church, so appointment suits the context better; there may have been a previous election, but the word cannot be held to imply one. Wesley marvels at the material, elders made of men newly converted: so soon can God enable even a babe in Christ to build up others.
24:
The homeward leg is mostly itinerary, and Clarke lays the whole of it out: from Derbe to Lystra, Lystra to Iconium, Iconium to the Pisidian Antioch, Antioch to Perga in Pamphylia, and Perga to Attalia, the journey crossing three provinces of Asia Minor. Calvin marks the turn, that being now about to return to the Antioch from which they were sent away they go through Pamphylia, the middle region toward Mount Taurus, with Perga and Attalia lying near together. Barnes notes only that these were places they had visited before, and Wesley that both were cities of Pamphylia.

Perga is where Ellicott finds a coincidence. On the outward journey nothing is said of their preaching there: we are simply told that Mark left them and that they went on. On the return, accordingly, they did what they had then left undone. Robertson reads the same silence the same way, that they now stopped and preached in a city where they had apparently not done so before. Calvin draws a different inference from the fact that the Word is said to be preached in the one place only, guessing that they had not opportunity offered them everywhere, since teaching was a thing they were wont to let pass nowhere. Gill supplies what would settle it: an ancient copy adds here that they preached the Gospel to the inhabitants of Attalia, and doubtless with success, though no mention is made of it here or elsewhere, nor of any church in the place. Ellicott takes the opposite view, that there is no record of work done there and they probably went only to find a sailing-vessel for Antioch, their ship passing between Cilicia and Cyprus to enter the Orontes at Seleucia.

Where Attalia stood is described four times and not quite alike. Robertson makes it the port of Perga, sixteen miles down the same river and capital of Pamphylia; Ellicott makes the visit a détour to a harbour at the mouth of a different river, since on the outward journey they had gone straight up to Perga from the coast. All agree on the founder, Attalus of Pergamus, who gave the town his own name; but the modern name comes out three ways in a century, Gill calling it Sattalia and noting the bay beside it where a considerable mart is held for the whole country and the tapestry the town is famous for, Barnes calling it Antali, and Robertson calling it Adala and long the chief harbour of the south coast of Asia Minor. Gill also cites an old authority that it was once the metropolis of Pamphylia, and reports a reading which makes the thing preached at Perga the word of the Lord. Robertson ends with a question nobody else asks: we do not know why they did not revisit Cyprus, unless because no permanent Gentile churches had been founded there.
26:
The phrase about being recommended to the grace of God settles a question. Barnes says it shows conclusively that the work first contemplated had been fully accomplished, and — his real point — that the setting apart at the outset was neither an ordination to the ministry nor an appointment to the apostleship, Paul having been an apostle already and Barnabas never one in the proper sense. Wesley reaches the same conclusion in a line, that this shows the nature and design of that laying on of hands. Calvin presses the wording: Luke might have said they were ordained there apostles of the Gentiles, but by a circumlocution he expresses more plainly that they were not sent away of men, their whole journey and its success being committed to God, so that the preaching was no man’s work but a work of the grace of God.

The homecoming meeting is Robertson’s scene. It was the first missionary meeting in history, he says, and not hard to convene once the news spread; the suitability of the Gospel to become the religion of the world had not before been put to the test. Ellicott adds that little had been heard of them meanwhile, and we may picture the eagerness with which Antioch gathered to listen. Barnes says the account was owed, the church having sent them out. Calvin and Clarke both insist on the grammar of the credit: Luke says not that they extolled what they had done but what the Lord had done by them, and Calvin goes to the preposition, refusing any sense that would make them partners with God.

On the door of faith, two of them hear Paul’s own voice. Ellicott calls it the first occurrence, in the chronological order of the books, of a characteristic phrase, a favourite metaphor of Paul’s, and thinks it a fragment from his speech; Robertson says the same from the other end, that Paul uses the figure three times in his letters, perhaps recalling the language used here. Ellicott then notes the phrase in the Revelation, where Paul and John are found agreeing that the door stood open wider than ever and that no man might shut it. Calvin will not let the door be a mere opportunity: it was set open not because the gospel was preached with the external voice, but because they were effectually called, since the kingdom is set open by preaching, but no man entereth save he to whom God reacheth out his hand. Robertson lists what the door was not: not law, not circumcision, not heathen philosophy or mythology.

How long the stay lasted nobody can say, and the guesses run wide. Ellicott reckons the words cover more than a year, in which the preaching drew together a large number of Gentile converts. Barnes counts from the dates: if these things fell about the year forty-five and the council at Jerusalem met in fifty-one or fifty-three, here is an interval of five to eight years of which we have no account, though Paul certainly made journeys unrecorded here, preaching as far as Illyricum, and we may be certain these men were not idle. Clarke agrees on five years passed over in perfect silence and fills them with the sufferings Paul lists but Luke does not: five scourgings, three beatings, three shipwrecks, and a night and a day in the deep. Gill offers a reason for the delay, the disputes with judaizing Christians about the law which the next chapter reports. Robertson closes on the balance of power: it was a happy time of fellowship, the experiment begun by the church of Antioch now a pronounced success, no sign of jealousy in Barnabas when Paul came home the chief hero, and a new centre of Christian activity in being — but what would Jerusalem think, since the two made no report to it at all?
